claim: Automatic tensor program auto-scheduling (DietCode) can reduce compilation time on dynamic-shape workloads
conditions: Language modeling workload; compared to existing tensor program auto-scheduler baseline
effect: Compilation time reduction up to 5.88×
evidence: Quantitative benchmark result
quote: DietCode reduce the compilation time by up to 5.88× on the state-of-the-art language modeling workload compared with the existing tensor program auto-scheduler
paper: Automatic Compiler-based Optimizations for Deep Neural Networks

claim: Compiler-based optimizations can incur measurable runtime overhead as a tradeoff cost
conditions: GPU memory footprint optimization (Echo); training state-of-the-art DNNs
effect: 1% runtime performance overhead from recomputation optimization
evidence: Quantitative overhead measurement
quote: we can significantly reduce the GPU memory footprint by up to 3.13× with only 1% runtime performance overhead
paper: Automatic Compiler-based Optimizations for Deep Neural Networks

claim: Graph breaks force execution to fall back to Python eager mode, introducing costly CPU-GPU synchronization
conditions: PyTorch 2 with TorchDynamo/TorchInductor; code patterns that cause graph breaks
effect: Costly CPU-GPU synchronization and reduced optimization opportunities leading to slower execution
evidence: Core finding from GraphMend investigation; identified as primary problem affecting compiled model performance
quote: certain code patterns still cause graph breaks that force execution to fall back to Python eager mode, introducing costly CPU-GPU synchronization and reducing optimization opportunities
paper: GraphMend: Code Transformations for Fixing Graph Breaks in PyTorch 2

claim: Cold-start compilation overhead differs dramatically from steady-state performance
conditions: PyTorch 2 torch.compile on NVIDIA GPUs; GraphMend-fixed models on 27 models with graph breaks
effect: Up to 26x cold-start speedup and 5x average, but only 1.39x steady-state forward pass speedup
evidence: Experimental measurements in GraphMend evaluation; direct comparison of cold vs. steady-state phases
quote: GraphMend achieves up to 26x cold-start speedup, 5x on average, and up to 1.39x steady-state forward pass speedup
paper: GraphMend: Code Transformations for Fixing Graph Breaks in PyTorch 2

claim: Graph breaks are prevalent in real model deployments despite PyTorch 2 improvements
conditions: Analysis of 195 HuggingFace transformer models; PyTorch 2 era
effect: 13.8% of production models contain unfixed graph breaks that silently degrade performance
evidence: Systematic investigation of HuggingFace model collection
quote: Our investigation of 195 Hugging Face models reveals that 13.8% of models exhibit graph breaks
paper: GraphMend: Code Transformations for Fixing Graph Breaks in PyTorch 2

claim: Eliminating graph breaks enables larger uninterrupted FX graphs and better optimization
conditions: Semantics-aware source-level transformations applied to graphs with breaks; PyTorch 2 compilation pipeline
effect: Improved performance through increased graph size and optimization opportunities without developer refactoring
evidence: GraphMend eliminated 107 of 147 graph breaks (73%), fully fixing all breaks in 21 models with measurable speedup
quote: These transformations enable PyTorch to capture larger, uninterrupted FX graphs without manual refactoring by developers
paper: GraphMend: Code Transformations for Fixing Graph Breaks in PyTorch 2

claim: Multi-scale augmentation (continuous resizing during training) achieves high performance without increased training time compared to single-size or curriculum learning strategies
conditions: ImageNet pre-trained ResNet models fine-tuned on calcaneus fracture x-ray radiographs (1,775 images); training on images resized between 128×128 and 900×900
effect: AUROC 0.938 (95% CI: 0.936–0.939) without increased training or inference time
evidence: Empirical measurement of AUROC and training time across strategies
quote: Multi-scale augmentation achieved the highest average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.938; 95% CI: 0.936–0.939) across image resolutions without increased training or inference time.
note: Tangentially relevant: shows resolution-aware training can decouple performance from training time cost
paper: Evaluation of resolution-aware training strategies for deep learning detection of calcaneus fractures on x-ray

claim: Curriculum learning (sequential training from low to high resolution) requires significantly longer training time despite improved sensitivity
conditions: Same ResNet setup; sequential training 128×128 → 900×900
effect: Training time 11.8 hours (IQR: 11.1–16.4) with improved sensitivity (85.4%–90.1% for in-distribution, 78.2%–89.2% for out-of-distribution)
evidence: Measured training time and sensitivity metrics
quote: Curriculum learning demonstrated the highest sensitivity for in-distribution low-resolution images (85.4%–90.1%) and out-of-distribution high-resolution images (78.2%–89.2%) but required significantly longer training times (11.8 [IQR: 11.1–16.4] hours; P <.001).
note: Shows schedule-based resolution changes increase computational cost
paper: Evaluation of resolution-aware training strategies for deep learning detection of calcaneus fractures on x-ray

claim: Existing augmentations and training approaches induce a significant discrepancy between the typical size of objects seen by the classifier at train versus test time
conditions: Image classification tasks with data augmentation; typical training-to-test scenario without explicit resolution alignment strategy
effect: This discrepancy degrades classification accuracy and creates a train-test mismatch that reduces performance
evidence: Experimental validation presented through systematic comparison of augmentation effects across train-test resolution pairs
quote: This paper first shows that existing augmentations induce a significant discrepancy between the typical size of the objects seen by the classifier at train and test time.
paper: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy

claim: For a target test resolution, using a lower training resolution offers better classification accuracy at test time
conditions: Target test resolution is fixed and known in advance; image classification on ImageNet; comparison across multiple training resolutions
effect: Improved accuracy at target test resolution: 77.1% ImageNet top-1 with ResNet-50 trained at 128×128, and 79.8% trained at 224×224
evidence: Direct experimental measurement on ImageNet with standard benchmarks
quote: We experimentally validate that, for a target test resolution, using a lower train resolution offers better classification at test time.
paper: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy

claim: Fine-tuning specifically at the target test resolution is an effective and efficient strategy to optimize classifier performance when train and test resolutions differ
conditions: When training and test resolutions differ; fine-tuning is computationally cheap; network pre-trained at different resolution
effect: Efficiently recovers and optimizes accuracy across resolution transitions; enables strong performance from small training images (e.g., 86.4% ImageNet top-1 for ResNeXt-101 pre-trained at 224×224 then fine-tuned for 320×320)
evidence: Experimental validation showing that cheap fine-tuning at target resolution achieves state-of-the-art results
quote: We then propose a simple yet effective and efficient strategy to optimize the classifier performance when the train and test resolutions differ. It involves only a computationally cheap fine-tuning of the network at the test resolution.
paper: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy

claim: Joint optimization of training and testing resolutions improves performance
conditions: ImageNet classification, EfficientNet models, fine-tuning at test resolution
effect: +0.5% to +2% absolute top-1 accuracy across model sizes
evidence: Tables 1-2 show systematic improvements; FixEfficientNet-B0 achieves 79.3% vs 77.6% baseline
quote: Touvron et al. show [1] that this separate optimization has a detrimental effect on the test-time performance of models. They address this problem with the FixRes method, which jointly optimizes the choice of resolutions and scales at training and test time
paper: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy: FixEfficientNet

claim: Training-test resolution mismatch arises from different Region of Classification sampling
conditions: Standard ImageNet preprocessing with random crops at train time, center crops at test time
effect: Skews data distribution seen by CNN between train and test
evidence: Described in Introduction as the core problem motivating FixRes
quote: Thus, while the crops extracted at training and test time have the same size, they arise from different RoCs, which skews the data distribution seen by the CNN.
paper: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy: FixEfficientNet

claim: Resolution-dependent fine-tuning is neutral to overfitting status
conditions: Fine-tuning only top layers at target resolution, same augmentation as FixRes
effect: Overfitted models remain overfitted; non-overfitted remain non-overfitted (no overfitting change)
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing relative model ordering on ImageNet vs ImageNet-V2
quote: The FixRes fine-tuning procedure is neutral with respect to overfitting: overfitted models remain overfitted and conversely.
paper: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy: FixEfficientNet

claim: Higher test resolution improves accuracy despite matching train resolution distribution
conditions: EfficientNet models, single-crop evaluation, fine-tuned from pre-trained weights
effect: Accuracy gains of +1.7% (B0), +1.8% (B8) on ImageNet with 300M unlabeled pretraining
evidence: Table 1 shows systematic gains across all model scales
quote: For instance, our FixEfficientNet-B0 trained without additional training data achieves 79.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 5.3M parameters. This is a +0.5% absolute improvement over the Noisy student EfficientNet-B0 trained with 300M unlabeled images.
paper: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy: FixEfficientNet

claim: Reducing training resolution with progressive fine-tuning at higher resolutions improves practical training efficiency
conditions: EfficientNet models, image classification task, Graphcore IPU accelerator
effect: Improved practical efficiency for both training and inference
evidence: Empirical finding stated in abstract
quote: reducing compute by lowering the training resolution and inexpensively fine-tuning at higher resolution. We find that these three methods improve the practical efficiency for both training and inference.
paper: Making EfficientNet More Efficient: Exploring Batch-Independent Normalization, Group Convolutions and Reduced Resolution Training

claim: Batch-independent normalization can match batch normalization performance with batch-independent statistics
conditions: EfficientNet models, image classification
effect: Maintains accuracy while enabling batch-independent training
evidence: Method proposal stated in abstract
quote: adding proxy-normalized activations to match batch normalization performance with batch-independent statistics
paper: Making EfficientNet More Efficient: Exploring Batch-Independent Normalization, Group Convolutions and Reduced Resolution Training

claim: Generalizing depthwise convolutions to group convolutions improves model efficiency
conditions: EfficientNet models, image classification
effect: Improved practical efficiency for training and inference
evidence: Method proposal stated in abstract
quote: generalising depthwise convolutions to group convolutions
paper: Making EfficientNet More Efficient: Exploring Batch-Independent Normalization, Group Convolutions and Reduced Resolution Training

claim: Progressive image size increase during training causes accuracy drop
conditions: Training with progressively increasing image resolution during training
effect: Accuracy drop
evidence: Empirical observation from paper
quote: Our training can be further sped up by progressively increasing the image size during training, but it often causes a drop in accuracy.
paper: EfficientNetV2: Smaller Models and Faster Training

claim: Adaptive regularization adjustment compensates for progressive learning accuracy loss
conditions: Progressive learning paired with adaptive adjustment of dropout and data augmentation
effect: Achieves both fast training and good accuracy despite progressive resolution scheduling
evidence: Proposed solution validated empirically on ImageNet and other datasets
quote: To compensate for this accuracy drop, we propose to adaptively adjust regularization (e.g., dropout and data augmentation) as well, such that we can achieve both fast training and good accuracy.
paper: EfficientNetV2: Smaller Models and Faster Training

claim: EMA enables implicit regularization through noise reduction, allowing convergence with higher learning rates than standard SGD without decaying to near-zero
conditions: SGD with momentum (0.9), cosine annealing LR schedule; CIFAR-100 on ResNet-18
effect: Convergence achieved with substantially higher final learning rates while maintaining or improving generalization
evidence: Experimental observation with visualization (Figure 1a-b) showing EMA peaks at epoch 150 with high LR before deteriorating
quote: Averaging during training is an alternative way of to reduce noise in SGD iterates and reach a good solution without too much learning rate decay. This allows to freely tune the final learning rate to control the strength of implicit regularization, while still converging to a good solution within the neighborhood.
paper: Exponential Moving Average of Weights in Deep Learning: Dynamics and Benefits

claim: EMA solutions are fundamentally different from SGD solutions, reaching different regions of the loss landscape that generalize better
conditions: General deep learning training with SGD trajectory
effect: Solutions with improved generalization, calibration, prediction consistency, and transfer learning over last-iterate SGD
evidence: Theoretical reasoning combined with experimental validation across multiple metrics
quote: We find that the solutions reached with EMA and early stopping are different from the baseline solution obtained by last-iterate momentum SGD, and conjecture that this is due to implicit regularization via stochastic noise, obtained through the use of larger step-sizes.
paper: Exponential Moving Average of Weights in Deep Learning: Dynamics and Benefits

claim: EMA (Exponential Moving Average) is a weight averaging regularization that helps learn flat optima for better generalization without extra computational cost
conditions: Deep neural networks (general DNNs)
effect: Better generalization without extra cost
evidence: Direct statement of EMA's properties as a weight averaging method
quote: Exponential Moving Average (EMA) is a widely used weight averaging (WA) regularization to learn flat optima for better generalizations without extra cost in deep neural network (DNN) optimization.
paper: Switch EMA: A Free Lunch for Better Flatness and Sharpness

claim: Switch EMA (SEMA)—switching EMA parameters back to the original model after each epoch—allows DNNs to reach generalization optima with better flatness-sharpness tradeoff
conditions: Deep neural networks with SEMA modification applied
effect: Improved tradeoff between flatness and sharpness at generalization optima
evidence: Theoretical and empirical demonstration claimed
quote: This work unveils the full potential of EMA with a single line of modification, i.e., switching the EMA parameters to the original model after each epoch, dubbed as Switch EMA (SEMA). From both theoretical and empirical aspects, we demonstrate that SEMA can help DNNs to reach generalization optima that better trade-off between flatness and sharpness.
paper: Switch EMA: A Free Lunch for Better Flatness and Sharpness

claim: SEMA improves final performance and convergence speed across diverse tasks without requiring extra test-time computation
conditions: Vision and language tasks: image classification, self-supervised learning, object detection, segmentation, image generation, video prediction, attribute regression, language modeling; with popular optimizers and networks
effect: Performance improvements and faster convergence (magnitude not specified in abstract)
evidence: Comprehensive experimental results across multiple tasks and model types
quote: Comprehensive results with popular optimizers and networks show that SEMA is a free lunch for DNN training by improving performances and boosting convergence speeds.
paper: Switch EMA: A Free Lunch for Better Flatness and Sharpness
